concept.concept_description: Sperner's lemma states that any proper coloring of a triangulated simplex with n+1 colors has at least one fully colored simplex. Specifically, given an n-player game with strategies S_1, ..., S_n, construct the n-simplex Delta = Delta(S_1 x ... x S_n) of mixed strategy profiles. Define a Sperner coloring of Delta by: color vertex v with color i if player i's best response to v is strategy i. By Sperner's lemma, there exists a fully colored simplex. The center of this simplex is an approximate Nash equilibrium (each player is approximately best-responding). Taking the limit as the triangulation gets finer gives an exact Nash equilibrium. Conjecture: this construction gives a constructive proof of Nash's theorem that yields a triangulation-based algorithm for finding Nash equilibria with complexity O(N^{n}) where N is the total number of pure strategies. Test: implement the Sperner-based algorithm for 2-player games and verify it finds all Nash equilibria. Impact: Nash equilibria are combinatorial fixed points. Sperner's lemma is the fundamental theorem of game theory.

concept.title: Sheaf-Theoretic Data Integration: When Databases Form a Sheaf
concept.concept_description: A database with missing entries is a partial section of a sheaf. The sheaf condition (gluing) says that if two partial sections agree on their overlap, they can be glued into a global section. Conjecture: the probability that a random database with missing rate r satisfies the sheaf condition (i.e., can be consistently filled in) is P(sheaf) = (1-r)^{C(n,k)} where n is the number of columns, k is the number of rows, and C(n,k) is the number of overlapping constraints. This means: for a database with n columns and k rows, the probability of consistent imputation drops exponentially with the number of overlapping constraints. The sheaf imputation method: fill in missing values by finding the closest global section of the data sheaf. This is equivalent to solving a constrained optimization problem where the constraints are the sheaf condition on every overlapping pair of feature subsets. Conjecture: sheaf imputation outperforms mean imputation and KNN imputation when the missing rate r < 0.5 and the number of features n > 10, because the sheaf condition provides exponentially many consistency constraints that other methods ignore. Test: generate synthetic databases with known ground truth, introduce missing values at rate r, compare sheaf imputation with mean, KNN, and MICE. Impact: data imputation is a sheaf cohomology problem. The sheaf condition is the natural consistency constraint for databases.

concept.lean_guess: Define the data sheaf: for a database with n features and m observations, the base space is the poset P of feature subsets (ordered by inclusion). The sheaf F assigns to each feature subset S the set of complete observations on features S. The restriction maps F(S) -> F(T) for T subset S project out the features in S\T. The sheaf condition: for any cover {S_i} of S, the following is an equalizer: F(S) -> prod_i F(S_i) ==> prod_{i,j} F(S_i cap S_j). This means: a global section exists iff local sections agree on overlaps. P(sheaf) = P(all overlapping constraints are consistent) = prod_{overlaps} P(consistent | missing) = prod_{overlaps} (1-r)^2 = (1-r)^{2*C(n,2)} for pairwise overlaps. More precisely: there are C(n,2) overlapping pairs of features. Each pair requires consistency of the two partial sections. P(consistent pair) = (1-r)^2 (both features present) + r^2 * P(consistent by chance) + 2*r*(1-r) * P(consistent partial). For random data: P(consistent by chance) ~ 1/k where k is the number of values. So P(sheaf) ~ (1 - r + r/k)^{C(n,2)}. For n > 10 and r < 0.5: P(sheaf) > (1-r)^{C(n,2)} > 0 if r < 1 - C(n,2)^{-1/n}. Sheaf imputation: find the global section s that minimizes ||s - data||^2 subject to s in H^0(F). This is a constrained optimization problem. Test: generate synthetic data from a known distribution, introduce MCAR missing values, compare imputation methods.

universality, topology, or quantum-computational completeness is made.**

  constructor
  · intro h
    have := congrArg (fun w : A => (↑v⁻¹ : K) • w) h
    simpa [smul_smul] using this
  · intro h; simp [h]

  simp +decide [mul_add, add_mul, smul_smul, smul_sub]

  rw [← sub_eq_zero, jonesOp_commutator, ← Units.val_mul, unit_smul_eq_zero_iff,

| 2 | `!![2,1;1,1]`     | `!![F3,F2;F2,F1]` |

| 5 | `!![8,5;5,3]`     | `!![F6,F5;F5,F4]` |

# A Non-Abelianity Certificate for Jones Braid Operators

## Abstract

We formalize, in Lean 4 with Mathlib, the precise algebraic mechanism that makes
Fibonacci / Jones braiding *non-abelian*. Working over an arbitrary field `K`
and an arbitrary (possibly noncommutative) `K`-algebra `A`, we study the Jones
operator attached to a Temperley–Lieb-type generator `X` and a unit `u : Kˣ`,

```
jonesOp u X = (u : K) • 1 + (↑u⁻¹ : K) • X.
```

Our two main results are an exact commutator identity and a sharp
*non-abelianity equivalence*: the Jones images of two generators commute if and
only if the generators themselves commute. This is deliberately **not** a
density or universality statement; it is the clean, fully verified algebraic core
on which such statements (in concrete representations) ultimately rest.

The contribution lives in
`Catalog/Physics/JonesBraidNonabelianCertificate.lean` and reuses the existing
catalog file `Catalog/Algebra/JonesTemperleyLiebBraid4.lean`.

## 1. Problem and motivation

Topological quantum computation encodes logical information in the braiding of
anyons. In the Fibonacci / Jones setting, the computational gates are the images
of the braid generators `σ_i` under a representation built from the
Temperley–Lieb algebra. A representation can only be computationally interesting
if it is **non-abelian**: if all braid images commuted, every circuit would
collapse to a diagonal (classical) action and no entangling gate could exist.

The usual story emphasizes the hard analytic fact that, for special parameter
values, the braid images are *dense* in a unitary group `SU(d)` (the
Freedman–Larsen–Wang universality theorem). That density result is genuinely
deep. But underneath it lies a far more elementary and completely general fact:
the Jones map does not *create* or *destroy* commutativity — it transports it
exactly. Two braid images commute precisely when the underlying Temperley–Lieb
generators do. Isolating and certifying this fact is the goal of this note.

## 2. Definitions

Fix a field `K`, a ring `A`, and a `K`-algebra structure `[Algebra K A]`. The
algebra `A` is allowed to be noncommutative (e.g. a matrix algebra).

* **Jones operator (this file).** For a unit `u : Kˣ` and `X : A`,
  ```
  jonesOp u X = (↑u : K) • 1 + (↑u⁻¹ : K) • X.
  ```
  Parametrizing by a *unit* `u` rather than a raw field element makes the
  invertibility of the relevant scalar (`↑u⁻¹`) structural rather than a
  side hypothesis.

* **Catalog Jones operator.** The existing catalog file defines, for a field
  element `A : K`,
  ```
  JonesTemperleyLiebBraid4.jonesOp A X = A • 1 + A⁻¹ • X.
  ```
  We connect the two via `jonesOp_eq_catalog` below; for a unit `u`,
  `jonesOp u X = JonesTemperleyLiebBraid4.jonesOp (↑u) X`.

## 3. Theorem statements

All statements are proved in full (no `sorry`, only the standard axioms
`propext`, `Classical.choice`, `Quot.sound`).

* **Scalar cancellation** (`unit_smul_eq_zero_iff`).
  For a unit `v : Kˣ` and `z : A`,
  ```
  (↑v : K) • z = 0  ↔  z = 0.
  ```

* **Exact commutator identity** (`jonesOp_commutator`).
  ```
  jonesOp u X * jonesOp u Y - jonesOp u Y * jonesOp u X
    = ((↑u⁻¹ : K) * (↑u⁻¹ : K)) • (X * Y - Y * X).
  ```

* **Non-abelianity equivalence** (`jonesOp_commute_iff`).
  ```
  jonesOp u X * jonesOp u Y = jonesOp u Y * jonesOp u X  ↔  X * Y = Y * X.
  ```

* **Specialization bridge** (`jonesOp_eq_catalog`).
  ```
  jonesOp u X = JonesTemperleyLiebBraid4.jonesOp (↑u : K) X.
  ```

* **Catalog corollary** (`catalog_jonesOp_commute_iff`).
  The same equivalence stated directly for the catalog operator.

* **Concrete example** (`exampleX_mul_exampleY_ne`,
  `example_jonesOp_noncommute`).
  With `X = !![0,1;0,0]` and `Y = !![0,0;1,0]` over `ℚ` we have `XY ≠ YX`, hence
  for *every* rational unit `u` the operators `jonesOp u X` and `jonesOp u Y` do
  not commute.

## 4. Proof sketches

**Scalar cancellation.** If `(↑v) • z = 0`, apply `(↑v⁻¹) •` to both sides; by
`smul_smul` the left side becomes `(↑v⁻¹ * ↑v) • z = (↑(v⁻¹ * v)) • z = 1 • z =
z` while the right side stays `0`. The converse is `smul_zero`.

**Commutator identity.** Unfold `jonesOp` and expand both products with
`mul_add`, `add_mul`, and `smul_smul`. The `1 • 1`, `X`, and `Y` terms are
identical in both orders (scalars in `K` commute), so they cancel under
subtraction. What remains is `(↑u⁻¹)² • (X*Y) - (↑u⁻¹)² • (Y*X)`, which equals
`(↑u⁻¹ * ↑u⁻¹) • (X*Y - Y*X)` by `smul_sub`. The bookkeeping of additive terms is
discharged by `abel`.

**Non-abelianity equivalence.** Rewrite `P = Q` as `P - Q = 0` (`sub_eq_zero`),
substitute the commutator identity, and observe `↑u⁻¹ * ↑u⁻¹ = ↑(u⁻¹ * u⁻¹)`
(`Units.val_mul`). Apply `unit_smul_eq_zero_iff` for the unit `u⁻¹ * u⁻¹` to drop
the nonzero scalar, leaving `X*Y - Y*X = 0`, i.e. `X*Y = Y*X`. This is exactly
the "injectivity of scalar multiplication by the nonzero scalar `(↑u⁻¹)²`"
mentioned in the problem statement.

**Bridge and corollary.** `jonesOp_eq_catalog` is `simp` after unfolding both
definitions, using `↑u⁻¹ = (↑u)⁻¹` in a field. The catalog corollary rewrites the
catalog operator back to `jonesOp u` and invokes the equivalence.

**Concrete example.** The matrix product inequality is settled by evaluating the
`(0,0)` entries (`1` vs `0`). The Jones conclusion is then *immediate* from the
equivalence — no further matrix computation is required, which is precisely the
point of having a bridge theorem.

## 5. Significance for topological quantum compiling

A compiler for a braiding-based architecture must reason about *when* two gates
commute (for scheduling, parallelization, and circuit identities) and must
certify that the gate set is genuinely non-classical. The equivalence
`jonesOp_commute_iff` provides both at the source level:

* commutation of Jones gates is *decidable from* commutation of the much simpler
  Temperley–Lieb generators, so commutation analysis can be pushed down to the
  generator algebra;
* a single non-commuting pair of generators certifies, with no further work,
  that the braid representation is non-abelian — the necessary precondition for
  any entangling gate.

Because the result holds over an arbitrary field and an arbitrary algebra, it
applies uniformly to every concrete model (matrix representations, fusion
categories realized as algebras, parameter specializations), and the verified
`ℚ`-matrix example shows the inference is effective.

## 6. Limitation: this is not a density theorem

We make this explicit. The results here say *nothing* about:

* density of braid images in `SU(d)` or any other group;
* universality for quantum computation;
* topology, anyons, or modular tensor categories beyond their algebraic shadow;
* the special parameter values (roots of unity) at which Fibonacci anyons live.

In particular, non-abelianity is *necessary* but not *sufficient* for
universality. The deep Freedman–Larsen–Wang density theorem is out of scope. What
we contribute is the rigorous, fully general algebraic bridge — *noncommuting
Temperley–Lieb generators give noncommuting Jones braid images, and conversely* —
on top of which density statements for specific representations can later be
built.

/-!
# Tropical Cryptography: Eigenvalue Cryptanalysis of the Tropical Discrete Log

This file formalizes the core mathematics behind the **Tropical Discrete Logarithm
Problem (TDLP)** and the proposed tropical Diffie–Hellman key exchange, building on
the min-plus matrix algebra in `Tropical.MinPlusAlgebra`.

## The scheme (informal)

Over the min-plus semiring `(ℝ, min, +)` one defines the tropical matrix power
`A^{⊗k}` by iterated `tropMatMul`. The proposed key exchange is:

* public `A`, Alice's secret `a`, Bob's secret `b`;
* Alice publishes `A^{⊗a}`, Bob publishes `A^{⊗b}`;
* shared key `A^{⊗ab}` recovered as `(A^{⊗b})^{⊗a} = (A^{⊗a})^{⊗b}`.

The **security conjecture** is that recovering `k` from `(A, A^{⊗k})` (the TDLP) is
hard.

## What we prove

The headline result is a *cryptanalytic* one: the TDLP is **not** hard whenever `A`
has a nonzero tropical eigenvalue. Concretely:

* `tropEigen_pow` — **eigenvalue additivity**: if `(λ, v)` is a tropical eigenpair
  of `A`, then `((k+1)λ, v)` is a tropical eigenpair of `A^{⊗k}`.
* `tdlp_break` — from the eigenvalue of `A^{⊗k}` on `v` the exponent `k` is uniquely
  determined when `λ ≠ 0`; hence the discrete log leaks.
* `tdlp_recover_formula` — the explicit recovery formula `k + 1 = μ / λ`.
* `tropDH_correct` — the key exchange is *correct*: the shared key is well defined,
  `(A^{⊗a})^{⊗b} = (A^{⊗b})^{⊗a}`.

These together say: the tropical DH protocol runs correctly, but its secret exponents
are recoverable by a single eigenvalue computation, refuting the security conjecture
for the eigenvalue-nondegenerate case.

This file reuses `tropMatMul`, `tropMatVecMul`, `IsTropicalEigenpair`,
`tropMatVecMul_shift`, and `tropMatMul_assoc` from `Tropical.MinPlusAlgebra`.

## References
* Grigoriev, D., Shpilrain, V. "Tropical cryptography" (2014).
* Kotov, M., Ushakov, A. "Analysis of a key exchange protocol based on tropical
  matrix algebra" (2018).
-/

open Finset Matrix

variable {n : ℕ} [NeZero n]

/-! ## Section 1: Tropical matrix power

We index by exponent-minus-one: `tropMatPow A k` denotes `A^{⊗(k+1)}`, the
`(k+1)`-fold tropical product of `A` with itself. This avoids needing a tropical
identity element (which over `ℝ` requires an unbounded "infinity" entry). -/

/-- `tropMatPow A k = A^{⊗(k+1)}`, the `(k+1)`-fold tropical (min-plus) power. -/
def tropMatPow (A : Matrix (Fin n) (Fin n) ℝ) : ℕ → Matrix (Fin n) (Fin n) ℝ
  | 0 => A
  | (k + 1) => tropMatMul A (tropMatPow A k)

@[simp] theorem tropMatPow_zero (A : Matrix (Fin n) (Fin n) ℝ) :
    tropMatPow A 0 = A := rfl

theorem tropMatPow_succ (A : Matrix (Fin n) (Fin n) ℝ) (k : ℕ) :
    tropMatPow A (k + 1) = tropMatMul A (tropMatPow A k) := rfl

/-! ## Section 2: Compatibility of matrix and matrix-vector products -/

/-
**Matrix–vector associativity**: `(A ⊗ B) ⊗ v = A ⊗ (B ⊗ v)`. The tropical
matrix-vector action is an action of the multiplicative semigroup of tropical
matrices.
-/
theorem tropMatVecMul_tropMatMul
    (A B : Matrix (Fin n) (Fin n) ℝ) (v : Fin n → ℝ) :
    tropMatVecMul (tropMatMul A B) v = tropMatVecMul A (tropMatVecMul B v) := by
  ext i;
  refine' le_antisymm _ _ <;> simp +decide [ tropMatVecMul, tropMatMul ];
  · intro j; obtain ⟨ k, hk ⟩ := Finset.exists_min_image Finset.univ ( fun k => B j k + v k ) ⟨ j, Finset.mem_univ j ⟩ ; use k;
    simp_all +decide [ Finset.inf'_le, Finset.le_inf' ];
    rw [ show ( Finset.univ.inf' Finset.univ_nonempty fun k => B j k + v k ) = B j k + v k from le_antisymm ( Finset.inf'_le _ <| Finset.mem_univ _ ) <| Finset.le_inf' _ _ fun x hx => hk x ] ; linarith [ Finset.inf'_le ( fun k_1 => A i k_1 + B k_1 k ) ( Finset.mem_univ j ) ];
  · intro b; have := Finset.exists_min_image Finset.univ ( fun k => A i k + B k b ) ⟨ b, Finset.mem_univ b ⟩ ; obtain ⟨ k, hk₁, hk₂ ⟩ := this; use k; simp_all +decide [ Finset.inf'_eq_csInf_image ] ;
    rw [ ← sub_le_iff_le_add ];
    refine' le_csInf _ _ <;> norm_num;
    · exact ⟨ _, ⟨ k, rfl ⟩ ⟩;
    · intro a; linarith [ hk₂ a, show sInf ( Set.range fun k_1 => B k k_1 + v k_1 ) ≤ B k b + v b from csInf_le ( Set.finite_range _ |> Set.Finite.bddBelow ) ( Set.mem_range_self _ ) ] ;

/-! ## Section 3: Power laws (semigroup structure) -/

/-
**Power product law**: `A^{⊗(a+1)} ⊗ A^{⊗(b+1)} = A^{⊗(a+b+2)}`.
-/
theorem tropMatMul_pow_pow (A : Matrix (Fin n) (Fin n) ℝ) (a b : ℕ) :
    tropMatMul (tropMatPow A a) (tropMatPow A b) = tropMatPow A (a + b + 1) := by
  induction' a with a ih generalizing b;
  · grind +locals;
  · grind +suggestions

/-
**Power of a power**: `(A^{⊗(a+1)})^{⊗(b+1)} = A^{⊗((a+1)(b+1))}`.
-/
theorem tropMatPow_tropMatPow (A : Matrix (Fin n) (Fin n) ℝ) (a b : ℕ) :
    tropMatPow (tropMatPow A a) b = tropMatPow A ((a + 1) * (b + 1) - 1) := by
  induction' b with b ih;
  · aesop;
  · convert tropMatMul_pow_pow A ( a ) ( ( a + 1 ) * ( b + 1 ) - 1 ) using 1;
    · rw [ ← ih, tropMatPow_succ ];
    · exact congr_arg _ ( Nat.sub_eq_of_eq_add <| by linarith [ Nat.sub_add_cancel ( by nlinarith : 1 ≤ ( a + 1 ) * ( b + 1 ) ) ] )

/-! ## Section 4: Tropical Diffie–Hellman correctness -/

/-
**Tropical DH correctness**: the shared key is well defined — Alice computing
`(A^{⊗b})^{⊗a}` and Bob computing `(A^{⊗a})^{⊗b}` obtain the same matrix.
-/
theorem tropDH_correct (A : Matrix (Fin n) (Fin n) ℝ) (a b : ℕ) :
    tropMatPow (tropMatPow A a) b = tropMatPow (tropMatPow A b) a := by
  rw [ tropMatPow_tropMatPow, tropMatPow_tropMatPow ];
  rw [ Nat.mul_comm ]

/-! ## Section 5: Eigenvalue additivity and the TDLP break -/

/-
The matrix-vector action of a power on an eigenvector scales by the exponent:
`A^{⊗(k+1)} ⊗ v = v + (k+1)λ`. This is `tropEigen_pow` in eigenpair language.
-/
theorem tropMatVecMul_pow_eigen
    (A : Matrix (Fin n) (Fin n) ℝ) (lam : ℝ) (v : Fin n → ℝ)
    (h : IsTropicalEigenpair A lam v) (k : ℕ) (i : Fin n) :
    tropMatVecMul (tropMatPow A k) v i = v i + (k + 1) * lam := by
  induction' k with k ih generalizing i;
  · simpa using h i;
  · convert
      ( show tropMatVecMul ( tropMatMul A ( tropMatPow A k ) ) v i =
          tropMatVecMul A ( fun j => v j + ( k + 1 ) * lam ) i from ?_ ) using 1;
    · have := tropMatVecMul_shift A v ( ( k + 1 ) * lam ) i;
      rw [ this, h i ] ; push_cast ; ring;
    · rw [ tropMatVecMul_tropMatMul ];
      exact congr_arg ( fun f => tropMatVecMul A f i ) ( funext ih )

/-
**Eigenvalue additivity**: if `(λ, v)` is a tropical eigenpair of `A`, then
`((k+1)λ, v)` is a tropical eigenpair of `A^{⊗(k+1)} = tropMatPow A k`.

This is the structural fact that makes the tropical discrete log easy: eigenvalues
are additive under powering.
-/
theorem tropEigen_pow
    (A : Matrix (Fin n) (Fin n) ℝ) (lam : ℝ) (v : Fin n → ℝ)
    (h : IsTropicalEigenpair A lam v) (k : ℕ) :
    IsTropicalEigenpair (tropMatPow A k) ((k + 1) * lam) v := by
  intro i; rw [ show ( ( k : ℝ ) + 1 ) * lam = ( k + 1 ) * lam by ring ] ; exact mod_cast tropMatVecMul_pow_eigen A lam v h k i;

/-
**TDLP break (uniqueness)**: if `A` has a nonzero tropical eigenvalue `λ` on
`v`, then any two powers of `A` that act on `v` by the same scalar `μ` must have the
same exponent. Hence the secret exponent in the tropical DH scheme is uniquely
determined by the eigenvalue of the published matrix — the discrete log leaks.
-/
theorem tdlp_break
    (A : Matrix (Fin n) (Fin n) ℝ) (lam : ℝ) (v : Fin n → ℝ)
    (h : IsTropicalEigenpair A lam v) (hlam : lam ≠ 0) (mu : ℝ) (a b : ℕ)
    (ha : IsTropicalEigenpair (tropMatPow A a) mu v)
    (hb : IsTropicalEigenpair (tropMatPow A b) mu v) :
    a = b := by
  -- From the eigenvalue equations, we have that $mu = (a + 1) * lam$ and $mu = (b + 1) * lam$.
  have hmu_a : mu = (a + 1) * lam := by
    have := tropMatVecMul_pow_eigen A lam v h a;
    linarith [ ha ⟨ 0, NeZero.pos n ⟩, this ⟨ 0, NeZero.pos n ⟩ ]
  have hmu_b : mu = (b + 1) * lam := by
    have := hb ⟨ 0, NeZero.pos n ⟩ ; have := @tropMatVecMul_pow_eigen n _ A lam v h b ⟨ 0, NeZero.pos n ⟩ ; aesop;
  exact_mod_cast ( mul_right_cancel₀ hlam <| by linarith : ( a : ℝ ) = b )

/-
**Explicit recovery formula**: from the public matrix `B = A^{⊗(k+1)}` one reads
off its eigenvalue `μ = (k+1)λ` on the shared eigenvector `v`, and recovers the
secret exponent via `k + 1 = μ / λ`.
-/
theorem tdlp_recover_formula
    (A : Matrix (Fin n) (Fin n) ℝ) (lam : ℝ) (v : Fin n → ℝ)
    (h : IsTropicalEigenpair A lam v) (hlam : lam ≠ 0) (k : ℕ) (mu : ℝ)
    (hmu : IsTropicalEigenpair (tropMatPow A k) mu v) :
    (k : ℝ) + 1 = mu / lam := by
  rw [ eq_div_iff hlam, mul_comm ];
  linarith [ hmu ⟨ 0, NeZero.pos n ⟩, tropMatVecMul_pow_eigen A lam v h k ⟨ 0, NeZero.pos n ⟩ ]

/-
The shared DH key acts on the common eigenvector by the *product* of the secret
exponents (plus the offsets): `((A^{⊗a})^{⊗b}) ⊗ v = v + ((a+1)(b+1)) λ`.
-/
theorem tropDH_shared_eigen
    (A : Matrix (Fin n) (Fin n) ℝ) (lam : ℝ) (v : Fin n → ℝ)
    (h : IsTropicalEigenpair A lam v) (a b : ℕ) :
    IsTropicalEigenpair (tropMatPow (tropMatPow A a) b) (((a + 1) * (b + 1) : ℕ) * lam) v := by
  convert tropEigen_pow ( tropMatPow A a ) ( ( a + 1 ) * lam ) v ( tropEigen_pow A lam v h a ) b using 1 ; push_cast ; ring

end

# Computational Evidence — Tropical Eigenvalue Additivity & TDLP

The objects live in the min-plus semiring `(ℝ, min, +)`; the matrix powers use
`inf'` over `ℝ`, which is **noncomputable** in Lean, so we give worked small cases by
hand (these directly motivated the formal statements that are now machine-proved in
`Core.lean`).

## 1. A 2×2 worked example of eigenvalue additivity

Let
```
A = [ 0   3 ]
    [ 2   0 ]   (min-plus)
```
Take the candidate eigenvector `v = (0, 0)` and `λ = 0`? Check:
`(A ⊗ v)_1 = min(0+0, 3+0) = 0`, `(A ⊗ v)_2 = min(2+0, 0+0) = 0`. So `(0, v)` is an
eigenpair — a *degenerate* spectrum, matching `zero_matrix_eigenzero`-style behaviour:
every power fixes `v`, no exponent leaks (cf. `eigenzero_no_leak`).

Now a **nondegenerate** example. Let
```
A = [ 5   3 ]
    [ 3   5 ]
```
with `v = (0,0)`. Then `(A ⊗ v)_i = min(5, 3) = 3`, so `(3, v)` is an eigenpair, `λ = 3`.

Tropical square `A^{⊗2} = A ⊗ A`:
`(A²)_{11} = min(5+5, 3+3) = 6`, `(A²)_{12} = min(5+3, 3+5) = 8`, symmetric.
```
A^{⊗2} = [ 6  8 ]
         [ 8  6 ]
```
`(A² ⊗ v)_i = min(6, 8) = 6 = 0 + 2·3`. Eigenvalue **doubled**: `λ(A^{⊗2}) = 6 = 2λ(A)`.

`A^{⊗3}`: `(A³)_{11} = min(6+5, 8+3) = 11`, so `(A³ ⊗ v)_i = min(11, 13) = 11`? Recompute
the off-diagonal: `(A³)_{12} = min(6+3, 8+5) = 9`, so `(A³ ⊗ v)_i = min(11, 9) = 9 = 3·3`.
Eigenvalue **tripled**: `λ(A^{⊗3}) = 9 = 3λ(A)`. ✓

This is exactly `tropMatVecMul_pow_eigen`: `λ(A^{⊗k}) = (k+1)λ` (index offset: our
`tropMatPow A k = A^{⊗(k+1)}`).

## 2. TDLP recovery check

Given the public `A` above (`λ = 3`) and a published `B = A^{⊗k}` with measured
eigenvalue `μ`:

| k (exponent) | μ = (k)·λ | recovered k = μ/λ |
|--------------|-----------|-------------------|
| 1            | 3         | 1                 |
| 2            | 6         | 2                 |
| 3            | 9         | 3                 |
| 10           | 30        | 10                |

Recovery is a single division — the formal content of `tdlp_recover_formula`. The
exponent is **never** hidden when `λ ≠ 0`, refuting the TDLP-hardness conjecture for
nondegenerate spectra.

## 3. Diffie–Hellman correctness check

Shared key exponent for secrets `a`, `b` (with our offset) is `(a+1)(b+1)`, symmetric
in `a, b`. E.g. `a=2, b=3 → 12`; `a=3, b=2 → 12`. Both parties land on `A^{⊗12}`,
confirming `tropDH_correct`.

## 4. Counterexample hunt

- Hunt for a nondegenerate (`λ ≠ 0`) instance where the eigenvalue is **not** additive
  under powering: none found; additivity is forced by `tropMatVecMul_shift` +
  associativity (now proved).
- Hunt for a `λ ≠ 0` instance where two distinct exponents share an eigenvalue on the
  same `v`: impossible, since `k ↦ (k+1)λ` is injective (`tdlp_break`).
- The **only** indistinguishability arises at `λ = 0` (`eigenzero_no_leak`), found
  immediately via the all-zeros / constant-diagonal matrices.

## OEIS note

The shared-key exponent table `(a+1)(b+1)` is just the multiplication table (no novel
integer sequence); no OEIS lookup is warranted. The eigenvalue sequence `k ↦ kλ` is a
trivial arithmetic progression. The interesting content is structural, not numeric,
which is why the formal proofs (not the numerics) are the deliverable.

double count, not an inequality. The average bound is what makes "some theorem is

namespace AntiGravity

open Finset

variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V]

/-- A dependency DAG on a (finite) set of theorems.  `dep a b` reads
"theorem `a` depends on theorem `b`"; `b` is the more fundamental theorem.
We model transitive reachability, hence a strict partial order. -/
structure DepDAG (V : Type*) where
  /-- `dep a b`: theorem `a` depends on theorem `b`. -/
  dep : V → V → Prop
  /-- Dependency is transitive (reachability composes). -/
  trans' : ∀ ⦃a b c⦄, dep a b → dep b c → dep a c
  /-- Nothing depends on itself (acyclicity). -/
  irrefl' : ∀ a, ¬ dep a a

open Classical in
/-- The finset of theorems that depend on `b`. -/
noncomputable def DepDAG.dependents (G : DepDAG V) (b : V) : Finset V :=
  univ.filter (fun a => G.dep a b)

/-- The **gravitational weight** of `b`: how many theorems depend on it. -/
noncomputable def DepDAG.weight (G : DepDAG V) (b : V) : ℕ := (G.dependents b).card

@[simp] lemma DepDAG.mem_dependents (G : DepDAG V) {a b : V} :
    a ∈ G.dependents b ↔ G.dep a b := by
  classical
  simp [DepDAG.dependents]

/-- **Gravitational monotonicity.** If `a` depends on `b`, then `b` is strictly
heavier than `a`: every dependent of `a` is a dependent of `b` (transitivity), and
`a` itself depends on `b` but not on itself. -/
theorem DepDAG.weight_lt_of_dep (G : DepDAG V) {u t : V} (h : G.dep u t) :
    G.weight u < G.weight t := by
  refine' Finset.card_lt_card _;
  simp_all +decide [ Finset.ssubset_def, Finset.subset_iff ];
  exact ⟨ fun x hx => G.trans' hx h, u, h, G.irrefl' u ⟩

open Classical in
/-- **Conservation law.** The total gravitational weight of the library equals the
number of dependency pairs. -/
theorem DepDAG.sum_weight_eq (G : DepDAG V) :
    ∑ b, G.weight b
      = (univ.filter (fun p : V × V => G.dep p.1 p.2)).card := by
  unfold DepDAG.weight
  simp +decide only [dependents, card_filter]
  exact Eq.symm (Fintype.sum_prod_type_right fun x => if G.dep x.1 x.2 then 1 else 0)

/-- There is always a maximally-heavy ("most foundational") theorem. -/
theorem DepDAG.exists_max_weight (G : DepDAG V) [Nonempty V] :
    ∃ b : V, ∀ a : V, G.weight a ≤ G.weight b := by
  simpa using Finset.exists_max_image Finset.univ ( fun a => G.weight a ) ( Finset.univ_nonempty )

/-- **Above-average foundation.** Some theorem carries at least the average weight:
its weight times the library size dominates the total weight. -/
theorem DepDAG.exists_weight_ge_average (G : DepDAG V) [Nonempty V] :
    ∃ b : V, (∑ a, G.weight a) ≤ Fintype.card V * G.weight b := by
  obtain ⟨ b, hb ⟩ := DepDAG.exists_max_weight G;
  exact ⟨ b, le_trans ( Finset.sum_le_sum fun _ _ => hb _ ) ( by simp +decide ) ⟩

/-- A theorem `b` is **anti-gravity** for thresholds `(wT, cT)` and cost
function `cost` if its weight is at least `wT` while its proof cost is at most
`cT`: high weight, short proof. -/
def DepDAG.IsAntiGravity (G : DepDAG V) (cost : V → ℕ) (wT cT : ℕ) (b : V) : Prop :=
  wT ≤ G.weight b ∧ cost b ≤ cT

end AntiGravity

# A finite infinitesimal probability model

This file builds, for each `n : ℕ`, a concrete finitely additive probability measure whose
values live in an ordered ring of *infinitesimals* rather than in `ℝ`.  The value type is the
ring of pairs `LexRat = ℚ × ℚ`, where a pair `(a, b)` is interpreted as the formal expression
`a + b·ε` with `ε` a positive infinitesimal.  Addition, subtraction and negation are the usual
componentwise operations on pairs, but the order is **lexicographic**: `(a₁, b₁) ≤ (a₂, b₂)` iff
`a₁ < a₂`, or `a₁ = a₂` and `b₁ ≤ b₂`.  Under this order `ε = (0, 1)` is positive but smaller than
every positive rational `(q, 0)`, i.e. it is a genuine infinitesimal.

## The model

The sample space for parameter `n` is `Option (Fin n)`.  The `n` "visible" atoms `some i` each
carry the infinitesimal weight `ε`, while the single "reservoir" atom `none` carries weight
`1 - n·ε`.  The reservoir weight is chosen exactly so that the total mass is

  `n · ε + (1 - n·ε) = 1`,

making the measure normalized.  Because the reservoir absorbs the deficit `-n·ε` in its
infinitesimal component while keeping a real component equal to `1`, it remains lexicographically
positive; meanwhile each visible atom has probability `ε`, which is positive yet infinitesimally
small — strictly below `1` and below every positive standard probability.

## Main results

* `LexRat.eps_infinitesimal` : `ε` is below every positive rational.
* `prob_eq_closed_form` : a closed form for the probability of an arbitrary event.
* `prob_nonneg` : every event has lexicographically nonnegative probability.
* `prob_union_disjoint` : finite additivity.
* `prob_univ` : the total mass is `1`.
* `visible_singleton_infinitesimal` : each visible atom has infinitesimal probability `ε < 1`.

/-- The value type of the infinitesimal probability model: a pair `(a, b)` read as `a + b·ε`. -/
abbrev LexRat := ℚ × ℚ

namespace LexRat

/-- Lexicographic `≤` on `LexRat`. -/
def lexLe (x y : LexRat) : Prop := x.1 < y.1 ∨ x.1 = y.1 ∧ x.2 ≤ y.2

/-- Lexicographic `<` on `LexRat`. -/
def lexLt (x y : LexRat) : Prop := x.1 < y.1 ∨ x.1 = y.1 ∧ x.2 < y.2

/-- Lexicographic nonnegativity: `(0,0) ≤ x`. -/
def Nonneg (x : LexRat) : Prop := lexLe (0, 0) x

/-- The unit `1 = (1, 0)`. -/
def one : LexRat := ((1 : ℚ), (0 : ℚ))

/-- The infinitesimal `ε = (0, 1)`. -/
def eps : LexRat := ((0 : ℚ), (1 : ℚ))

def ofRat (q : ℚ) : LexRat := (q, 0)

@[simp] lemma one_snd : one.2 = 0 := rfl
@[simp] lemma eps_fst : eps.1 = 0 := rfl
@[simp] lemma eps_snd : eps.2 = 1 := rfl
@[simp] lemma ofRat_fst (q : ℚ) : (ofRat q).1 = q := rfl
@[simp] lemma ofRat_snd (q : ℚ) : (ofRat q).2 = 0 := rfl

theorem eps_pos : lexLt (0, 0) eps := by

concept.title: The Library of Babel: Combinatorics of the Universal Library
concept.concept_description: Borges' Library of Babel contains every possible 410-page book — approximately 25^{1312000} volumes. The library is finite but vast beyond comprehension. Formalize the Library as the set of all strings over a 25-symbol alphabet of length 1312000. Conjecture: The probability that a random volume contains a meaningful proof of a given theorem T is approximately |T| * 25^{-k} where |T| is the length of T and k is the proof complexity of T. Moreover, the Library contains a universal catalog — a single volume that encodes the location of every other volume — and this catalog can be found in polynomial time using a variant of the de Bruijn sequence construction. The deepest question: does the Library contain its own complete catalog? By a diagonal argument, no single volume can encode all volumes (since 25^{1312000} > 1312000 * log_2(25^{1312000})). But a DISTRIBUTED catalog spanning N volumes can encode the entire Library if N > 25^{1312000} / (1312000 * log_2(25)). Test: compute the exact probability of finding a valid Lean 4 proof of a specific theorem in the Library. Construct a de Bruijn-based catalog for a mini-Library with alphabet size 4 and book length 16. Impact: the mathematics of universal information spaces — every possible text exists, but finding meaning requires a guide.
